Impact of Noise Pollution on Urban Ecosystems

A study of Punjab using published noise data

IntroductionLegal limitsNoise in PunjabGraphsEffectsDocumentaryCheck a levelMore toolsSolutionsQuizGlossaryReferences

Introduction

Noise is unwanted sound, and it is measured in decibels (dB). Because the decibel scale is logarithmic, a rise of 10 dB means the sound is about ten times more intense. In cities, noise comes mainly from road traffic and horns, loudspeakers at events, construction, industry, generators and festival fireworks.

An urban ecosystem includes more than people. It also covers birds, insects, stray and domestic animals, roadside trees and the soil around them. This project looks at how noise affects all of these in Punjab, and compares published noise levels with the legal limits.

Legal noise limits in India

The Noise Pollution (Regulation and Control) Rules, 2000 set limits for four zones. Day is 6 am to 10 pm and night is 10 pm to 6 am.

ZoneDay (dB)Night (dB)
Industrial7570
Commercial6555
Residential5545
Silence zone (hospitals, schools, courts)5040

Noise in Punjab: what has been recorded

These are published figures from news reports and official documents. They are not our own measurements. Years are given where the source states them.

Residential areas across Punjab. Against the permissible 55 dB, noise in residential areas of different Punjab cities varied between 75 and 90 dB over two years, according to PPCB data reported in 2013.
Jalandhar on Diwali. Residential noise averaged 72.7 dB in 2012 and about 71 dB in 2013 and 2014, and reached 82 to 85 dB between 9 and 11 pm on Diwali night in the year reported. Commercial areas averaged 73.6 dB in 2012.
Ludhiana, industry near homes. A joint committee report in a National Green Tribunal case found one industrial unit at 70.8 dB(A) even with noise controls, above the residential standard.
Who monitors. The Punjab Pollution Control Board (PPCB) monitors noise in cities such as Amritsar, Jalandhar, Ludhiana, Patiala and Mohali around Diwali. A PPCB engineer in Amritsar said most complaints concern religious functions on roads, with industry the other major source.
Rules on loudspeakers. Noise is to be controlled between 10 pm and 6 am under Supreme Court orders. Firecrackers must not exceed 125 dB at the point of bursting.

We found no published PPCB noise readings specific to Kapurthala, so this project uses figures from other Punjab cities.

Effects on the urban ecosystem

Birds and insects

Many urban birds sing louder or at higher pitch to be heard over traffic, which costs energy. Studies also link constant noise to lower breeding success and fewer birds near busy roads. Insects that communicate by sound, such as crickets, are affected too.

Mammals and stray animals

Sudden loud sounds like firecrackers and horns cause panic and stress in dogs, cattle and other animals, and can drive them away from habitats near cities.

Plants and the food chain

When noise drives away birds and insects that pollinate flowers or spread seeds, urban trees and plants can be affected indirectly.

Humans

Long exposure to noise raises hypertension risk, disturbs sleep, harms concentration in students and can damage hearing. The World Health Organization recommends keeping road traffic noise below 53 dB (day-evening-night average).

The chemistry link

The body treats loud noise as a stressor. The adrenal glands release stress hormones, mainly cortisol and adrenaline, which raise heart rate and blood pressure. When this happens repeatedly, the effect on health becomes chronic. Road traffic, the biggest source of noise, also releases CO, NOx and particulate matter, so noise and air pollution often hit the same places together.

Our documentary

As part of this project our group also made a short documentary. It follows a house sparrow living above a packed industrial junction in Ludhiana, and shows how noise that people have stopped noticing still affects the birds and animals around them. It ties together the effects described above.

Check a sound level against the law

Pick the type of area and the time of day, then enter a level from any decibel meter. The page shows how it compares with the legal limit.

Limits come from the table in the legal limits section. Phone decibel meters are only indicative.

More tools

How long is it safe to listen?

Enter a steady sound level to see the longest daily exposure recommended by NIOSH. It starts at 8 hours for 85 dB(A), and every 3 dB more halves the time.

This is an occupational guideline for adults, so it is a rough guide for everyday exposure. Below 85 dB it gives no limit.

What happens when two sounds add up?

Decibels cannot be added like ordinary numbers because the scale is logarithmic. Enter two levels to see the combined level.

Combined level = 10 x log10(10^(L1/10) + 10^(L2/10)). Two equal sounds add only 3 dB.

Solutions

  • Enforce horn restrictions and loudspeaker timings, especially near hospitals and schools.
  • Plant dense tree belts along busy roads, since foliage absorbs part of the sound.
  • Mark and sign silence zones clearly, and regularly publish noise readings.
  • Promote festivals with fewer high-decibel crackers, and keep to the 125 dB limit.
  • Insulate industrial units and keep them away from residential areas.

Glossary

Decibel (dB)

The unit used to measure sound level. It is logarithmic, so every 10 dB is ten times the sound intensity.

dB(A)

A decibel reading weighted to match how the human ear responds to different pitches. Noise limits are usually given in dB(A).

Silence zone

An area within 100 metres of hospitals, educational institutions and courts, where the lowest limits apply.

PPCB

The Punjab Pollution Control Board, the state body that monitors pollution, including noise.

Cortisol

A stress hormone released by the adrenal glands. Repeated noise stress keeps it raised, which is linked to health problems.

Ambient noise

The overall background sound in a place, made up of all nearby sources together.
